units.text: The app says the disk is full. Before resizing anything, identify the exact E B S volume and check the guest partition and filesystem. That tells you which layer actually needs to grow.
Before modifying the volume, create an appropriate recovery point. An E B S snapshot protects a point in time; make sure it represents recoverable application data if the workload requires that.

Increase the E B S capacity and check the modification state. At optimizing or completed, the larger size is ready for the guest. You don't need to wait for optimization to finish before extending the filesystem.
The disk can report more blocks while the filesystem still reports the old size. Extend a partition if there is one, then grow the existing filesystem with its own procedure. Don't format the volume.

Use the device and filesystem checks shown, then confirm the application can use the extra space. If the block device grew but the filesystem did not, finish the guest step rather than modifying E B S again.

For the sharing test, each client reaches a mount target over N F S on T C P port twenty forty-nine. Allow the intended source at the mount target and verify the network path before troubleshooting file permissions.

These two paths converge on the same Regional E F S filesystem. When using I A M authorization and an access point, use the E F S mount helper with T L S and check the effective identity and file permissions.

Have client A write orders dot C S V. Then ask client B to read it through the other mount target. Finally try the unauthorized client and confirm it is denied. A successful mount alone cannot answer all three questions.
What do you actually need back: the disk contents or an instance you can launch? For disk contents, restore a snapshot into a new volume. It gives you the saved blocks, not the launch settings.
When you need a bootable replacement, use an E B S-backed A M I. It references the snapshots and includes the image and block-device mappings. Choose the instance type at launch.
A recovery in another Region needs an available copy in that Region. For an encrypted copy, verify the destination key and permissions. Test the volume restore or instance launch before an outage.
Suppose only production volumes should be protected by this custom D L M policy. Tag the supported targets to define that scope. Do not assume that default policies use the same tag-targeting model.
Set the capture schedule for the recovery points this policy owns. Match the frequency to how much recent work the workload can afford to lose.
Define retention for the snapshots or E B S-backed A M Is it creates. It does not simply adopt existing snapshots from unrelated workflows or manage instance-store A M Is.
Configure copy actions where the selected policy and destination support them. If you instead need centrally managed protection across several supported services, evaluate A W S Backup.

The team already needs Windows shares and must choose storage for the access pattern. If many users open small files and browse directories, S S D fits the latency and metadata work. For broad sequential reads with tighter cost constraints, consider H D D and test the workload.
Changing storage media does not change the interface. The Windows clients still use S M B and Active Directory identities, and the file operations still need the right Windows permissions.

Now compare the parallel compute job. Many workers read a dataset over Lustre at once. Size not just the disk capacity, but also how quickly they can open files and how much aggregate data they can read.

On a supported deployment, use S three as a repository for source data or exported results. Workers still open files on Lustre. Export must be configured and verified before you rely on S three holding the output.

The on-premises app needs an S M B path even though the destination is S three. Users open a share on the gateway. With Active Directory authentication, the gateway can identify the Windows users instead of giving each user S three credentials.
The gateway runs on a supported virtual host. Its local cache helps serve file operations and can hold pending uploads. A local write can finish before its object appears in the bucket.

The gateway uses its I A M role to write objects to the S three bucket. Give that role the permissions the share needs and verify a test file arrives; an S M B login alone does not prove S three delivery.
Size the cache for the burst of writes the gateway may need to buffer. If clients write faster than it uploads, dirty data builds up in the local cache.
Monitor upload activity and gateway health. For a new deployment, use a supported host; the former A W S hardware appliance is not offered, and F S x File Gateway is unavailable to new customers.

A database is actively writing. A disk snapshot preserves blocks at a point in time, but those blocks could reflect an operation the database has not finished yet. How do you capture a state it can recover cleanly?
Use the database's supported pause or flush procedure. The point is to get the relevant writes to disk and stop the application from changing the state while the capture point is established.
Coordinate the snapshots of the volumes the database depends on. If data and logs live on separate disks, taking unrelated cuts can leave the recovered workload with pieces from different moments.

Resume writes once the application-specific procedure says the capture point has been established. You generally do not have to detach the volume, and you do not need to keep the app paused for the entire background upload.
Restore into a test instance and verify the database can open and use its data. A snapshot marked complete proves that E B S captured blocks, not that the application can recover from them.
A restored disk can be attached before every block is initialized. On demand, the first read of an unloaded block takes longer while E B S fetches it. Later reads can use the now-loaded block.

What if that first-read delay is unacceptable? Enable Fast Snapshot Restore on the snapshot in the target Availability Zone before creating the volume. An eligible restored volume then starts fully initialized.

Provisioned initialization gives you a background rate, not an instant warm disk. Choose a supported rate from one hundred to three hundred mebibytes per second and plan for how long the blocks take to load.
If you specify a provisioned rate on a snapshot that also has Fast Snapshot Restore, the provisioned rate takes precedence. Choose the behavior you actually want rather than setting both.

Two apps need the same filesystem but shouldn't see the same root. App A mounts through its access point. E F S applies that point's effective user and group and presents the app's directory as its root.
App B uses another access point with its own identity and root. It reaches the same E F S filesystem but starts in a different directory, so it doesn't work from the same view as App A.
These two paths end on one filesystem, not on two copies. Test by mounting each access point and checking that each app sees its intended files using its assigned identity.

Does creating the access point prevent another route? Not by itself. Configure I A M and filesystem policy to require the intended access point for the client, then verify a connection outside that policy does not gain access.

The default E F S filesystem policy grants the N F S path to network-reachable anonymous clients; it does not authenticate the caller with I A M. Being reachable still does not grant access through a blocked network path or to every file.

If the mount uses I A M and T L S, the client actions control mount, write and root privileges. Give the role only what its workload needs. Permission to mount is not automatically permission to write.
Both routes still reach a Pozix check. A client might be allowed to mount but denied when it opens a directory it does not own and cannot read. Check the effective user, group and mode on that path.
